prompt: At its simplest, what happens in an olefin metathesis reaction?

choices.text: Two alkenes exchange the substituents on their double bonds
An alkene adds H2 across its double bond
choices.why: That is hydrogenation. In metathesis, two alkenes swap the groups on their double-bond carbons.

choices.text: Two alkenes join to form a cyclobutane product
choices.why: A four-membered ring does form, but it contains the metal and opens again at once. The products are new alkenes.

choices.text: An alkene is cleaved into two carbonyl compounds
choices.why: Metathesis gives alkenes, not carbonyl compounds.

explanation: At its simplest, an olefin metathesis reaction is two olefins (alkenes) exchanging substituents on their double bonds. Its development earned Yves Chauvin, Robert Grubbs, and Richard Schrock the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

prompt: What general structure do olefin metathesis catalysts, such as the Grubbs catalyst, have?

choices.text: M=CH–R, a carbon–metal double bond, usually to ruthenium
A titanium compound combined with triethylaluminum
choices.why: That is a Ziegler–Natta catalyst (Section 31.2).

choices.text: An organolithium, R–Li
choices.why: Organolithiums such as butyllithium start anionic polymerization (Section 31.1).

choices.text: A peroxide, RO–OR
choices.why: Peroxides are radical initiators. Metathesis catalysts contain a metal–carbon double bond.

explanation: Olefin metathesis catalysts, such as the Grubbs catalyst now in common use, contain a carbon–metal double bond, usually to ruthenium (Ru), and have the general structure M=CH–R.

prompt: In olefin metathesis, the catalyst reacts with an alkene to form a metal-containing ring called a metallacycle. How many atoms make up this ring?
explanation: The catalyst reacts reversibly with an alkene to form a four-membered, metal-containing intermediate called a metallacycle, which immediately opens to give a different catalyst and a different alkene (Figure 31.5.1).

prompt: What happens to the metallacycle intermediate in olefin metathesis?

choices.text: It immediately opens to give a different catalyst and a different alkene
It is the final product and is isolated
choices.why: The metallacycle is an intermediate. It opens right away, so metathesis products are alkenes.

choices.text: It loses the metal to give a cyclobutane
choices.why: The ring opens to a new metal–carbon double bond and a new alkene, not a cyclobutane.

choices.text: It adds a proton to give a carbocation
choices.why: No carbocation is involved. The ring simply opens in a different direction from how it formed.

explanation: The catalyst reacts reversibly with an alkene to form a four-membered metallacycle, which immediately opens to give a different catalyst and a different alkene. The repeating ring-forming and ring-opening steps then continue (Figure 31.5.1).

prompt: Olefin metathesis exchanges the substituents on two alkenes' double bonds. Which new alkene forms from metathesis of CH3CH=CHCH3 with CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3?

choices.text: CH3CH=CHCH2CH3
CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3
choices.why: Metathesis only swaps the halves of the double bonds; it adds no hydrogen. The product is an alkene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH3, not the alkane pentane.

choices.text: CH3CH=CH2
choices.why: No CH2= end is present in either reactant, so propene can't form. The swap gives CH3CH=CHCH2CH3.

choices.text: CH3CH2CH2CH=CHCH3
choices.why: Neither reactant has a propyl group. Combining a CH3CH= half with a CH3CH2CH= half gives CH3CH=CHCH2CH3.

explanation: In metathesis the two double bonds are cut and the halves are swapped. CH3CH=CHCH3 is made of two CH3CH= halves, and CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3 of two CH3CH2CH= halves, so the crossed product is CH3CH=CHCH2CH3 (2-pentene).

prompt: In ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), what kind of monomer is used, and what drives formation of the polymer?

choices.text: A moderately strained cycloalkene such as cyclopentene; the ring strain favors ring-opening
An open-chain diene such as 1,8-nonadiene; escape of ethylene gas drives the reaction
choices.why: That describes ADMET, the second method in the section.

choices.text: A vinyl monomer with an electron-withdrawing group; a base starts the chain
choices.why: That describes anionic polymerization (Section 31.1).

choices.text: A diol and a diisocyanate; loss of CO2 drives the reaction
choices.why: That describes polyurethane formation (Section 31.4).

explanation: ROMP uses a moderately strained cycloalkene, such as cyclopentene. The strain of the ring favors ring-opening, thereby driving formation of the open-chain product.

prompt: What feature of a polymer made by ROMP allows further hydrogenation or functionalization?

choices.text: Double bonds spaced regularly along the chain
Small rings left intact along the chain
choices.why: The rings are opened during ROMP. What remains are double bonds spaced along the chain.

choices.text: Metal atoms bonded to every repeat unit
choices.why: The metal is part of the catalyst, not the repeat units. The polymer keeps regularly spaced C=C bonds.

choices.text: Hydroxyl groups at regular intervals
choices.why: Cyclopentene has no oxygen. The useful feature is the C=C bonds along the chain.

explanation: The polymer that results from ROMP has double bonds spaced regularly along the chain, allowing for either hydrogenation or further functionalization if desired.

prompt: In acyclic diene metathesis (ADMET) of a substrate such as 1,8-nonadiene, what drives the equilibrium toward polymer?

choices.text: The gaseous ethylene by-product escapes
The ring strain of the substrate favors ring-opening
choices.why: That is the driving force for ROMP. ADMET substrates are open-chain, with no ring strain.

choices.text: Water is removed as it forms
choices.why: No water forms. The by-product of ADMET is ethylene gas.

choices.text: CO2 bubbles out of the mixture
choices.why: CO2 is lost in polyurethane foaming (Section 31.4), not in ADMET.

explanation: ADMET involves olefin metathesis of an open-chain substrate with two double bonds at the ends of a long chain, such as 1,8-nonadiene. As the reaction proceeds, the gaseous ethylene by-product escapes, driving the equilibrium toward polymer. Polymers with molecular weights as high as 80,000 amu have been made this way.

prompt: ADMET polymerization of 1,8-nonadiene, H2C=CH(CH2)5CH=CH2, joins the molecules end to end and releases one ethylene, H2C=CH2, for each new link. How many carbon atoms are in each repeat unit of the polymer?
explanation: 1,8-Nonadiene has 9 carbons. Each time two terminal =CH2 ends combine they leave as ethylene, which removes 2 carbons per monomer, so each repeat unit is –CH=CH–CH2CH2CH2CH2CH2–, with 9 − 2 = 7 carbons.

prompt: Besides the double bonds in the products, why are ROMP and ADMET particularly valuable ways to make polymers?

choices.text: The metathesis reaction is compatible with many different functional groups in the monomer
They need no catalyst
choices.why: Both methods need a metathesis catalyst, such as the Grubbs catalyst.

choices.text: They work only with monomers that have no functional groups
choices.why: This is the reverse. Metathesis tolerates many different functional groups in the monomer.

choices.text: They always give perfectly isotactic polymers
choices.why: The section says nothing about tacticity here. Their value is functional-group compatibility plus the double bonds available for further work.

explanation: The ROMP and ADMET procedures are particularly valuable because the metathesis reaction is compatible with many different functional groups in the olefin monomer, and the double bonds in the polymers allow further manipulation.
